summary.text: Taking \(n=14\), the condition that \(2k+1\) be prime leaves only \(k=1,2,3,5,6,8,9,11\); the prime-count pairs in the adjacent intervals are respectively \((6,3),(3,4),(4,3),(3,4),(4,2),(4,1),(1,4),(2,3)\). None are equal, so the strengthened existence claim fails at \(n=14\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\pi(x)\) denote the number of primes less than or equal to \(x\). We disprove the strengthened existence assertion in the conjecture by taking
\[
n=14.
\]
This is an admissible value because \(14>1\) and \(14\ne 8\).

If the conjecture were true, there would therefore be an integer \(k\) such that
\[
0<k<14,
\]
\(2k+1\) is prime, and
\[
\pi(14k)-\pi(14(k-1))
=
\pi(14(k+1))-\pi(14k).
\tag{1}
\]
The difference on the left of (1) is the number of primes in
\((14(k-1),14k]\), and the difference on the right is the number of primes in
\((14k,14(k+1)]\). We show exhaustively that no such \(k\) exists.

The following table lists, for every possible value \(1\le k\le 13\), all the primes in those two adjacent intervals. The two numbers in the final column are their respective cardinalities.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
k&2k+1&\text{primes in }(14(k-1),14k]&
\text{primes in }(14k,14(k+1)]&\text{counts}\\ \hline
1&3&2,3,5,7,11,13&17,19,23&6,3\\
2&5&17,19,23&29,31,37,41&3,4\\
3&7&29,31,37,41&43,47,53&4,3\\
4&9&43,47,53&59,61,67&3,3\\
5&11&59,61,67&71,73,79,83&3,4\\
6&13&71,73,79,83&89,97&4,2\\
7&15&89,97&101,103,107,109&2,4\\
8&17&101,103,107,109&113&4,1\\
9&19&113&127,131,137,139&1,4\\
10&21&127,131,137,139&149,151&4,2\\
11&23&149,151&157,163,167&2,3\\
12&25&157,163,167&173,179,181&3,3\\
13&27&173,179,181&191,193&3,2
\end{array}
\]

For completeness, this table is a direct finite primality enumeration up to \(196=14\cdot14\). It can be checked by trial division: for every number at most \(196\), a composite number has a prime divisor at most \(\sqrt{196}=14\), so it suffices to test divisibility by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\). Testing these divisors gives exactly the primes displayed in the table. Thus the table gives exact interval counts, not merely lower or upper bounds.

Now impose the additional condition that \(2k+1\) be prime. As \(k\) ranges from \(1\) through \(13\), the values of \(2k+1\) are the odd numbers from \(3\) through \(27\). The prime ones are
\[
3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23,
\]
which correspond respectively to
\[
k\in\{1,2,3,5,6,8,9,11\}.
\]
(The excluded odd values are visibly composite: \(9=3^2\), \(15=3\cdot5\), \(21=3\cdot7\), \(25=5^2\), and \(27=3^3\).)

Reading the two interval counts from the table for precisely those eight admissible values gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
k&
\bigl(\pi(14k)-\pi(14(k-1)),\ 
\pi(14(k+1))-\pi(14k)\bigr)\\ \hline
1&(6,3)\\
2&(3,4)\\
3&(4,3)\\
5&(3,4)\\
6&(4,2)\\
8&(4,1)\\
9&(1,4)\\
11&(2,3).
\end{array}
\]
In every row the two entries are unequal, so equation (1) fails for every \(k\) for which \(2k+1\) is prime. Indeed, the full table shows that equality of the two interval counts occurs only at \(k=4\) and \(k=12\), but at those values \(2k+1\) is respectively \(9\) and \(25\), neither of which is prime.

Consequently, for \(n=14>1\), with \(14\ne8\), there is no positive integer \(k<14\) satisfying both the primality condition and the equality of adjacent prime counts. This directly contradicts the conjecture's “moreover” clause. It is immaterial whether the separate assertion \(a(14)>0\) holds: the conjecture asserts both that positivity statement and the strengthened existence statement, and the latter already fails at \(n=14\). Hence the stated conjecture is false.
